# Build it to run without you

Source: https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-27 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A GTM system is only an asset if the company owns it: the accounts, the records, the routines and the reasons. Knowledge walks out with people, platforms decide ownership by whose business holds the account, and EU law now backs the right to export from software providers. Build for handover from day one, write handover into any outside scope, and score yourself on ten questions to find and fix the weakest link first.

A GTM system is only an asset if the company owns it: the accounts, the records, the routines and the reasons. Most firms lose the last two first. A Panopto survey estimated 42% of institutional knowledge is unique to the individual in the role, so it leaves when they do. Build for handover from day one, write handover into any outside scope, then score yourself across all ten parts of this series and fix the weakest link first.

This is Part 10 of [Raise, Rally, Revenue](https://lowob.com/research/raise-rally-revenue/), the series that treats fundraising, community and customers as one commercial system. The first nine parts build the system. This one makes sure the company keeps it.

## What "owning it" means

| Asset | What to own | Common failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accounts | Ad, social, email, analytics, domain, community admin rights, all in the company's name | Agency or ex-employee holds the logins |
| Records | Evidence log, investor pipeline, partner list, customer source data | Spread across personal inboxes and DMs |
| Routines | Runbooks for recurring work: investor update, partner launch, community ritual, monthly report | Only one person knows how it's done |
| Reasons | Why each major decision was made and what was rejected | The next hire repeats an experiment that already failed |

The last row is the one almost nobody keeps, and the one that saves the most money. A decision record of three lines is enough: what we chose, what we rejected, what would change our minds.

## Why the reasons row matters most

Software teams formalised this problem fifteen years ago. In 2011 Michael Nygard proposed the architecture decision record: a short, numbered note per significant decision, with its context, the decision, its status and its consequences. His argument was that a newcomer who does not know why a decision was made has two bad options, to accept it blindly or reverse it blindly. Superseded records are kept, not deleted, so the history stays readable.

Commercial teams face the same choice every time someone leaves. Panopto's 2018 survey of 1,000 workers estimated that 42% of institutional knowledge is unique to the individual in the role, and that knowledge workers spent 5.3 hours a week waiting for information from colleagues or recreating it. In a small GTM team, the person who knows why the paid channel was cut, or why a partner was dropped, is often the founder or the agency. Our explainer on [what a decision record is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) sets out the fields and how to write one well.

> A good partner should be trying to make themselves unnecessary for the work they've finished.

## Accounts: ownership is decided by whose name is on them

Ownership of an ad or analytics account is not a matter of goodwill. It is how the platforms are built. Meta's business tools treat the business that owns an asset as the one that controls it: the owner grants a partner agency access to named tasks, such as advertising or analysis, and can remove the agency from the asset. An agency cannot pass on access to assets it only holds as an agency. If the agency opened the account in its own business, the company is the guest.

Large advertisers have noticed. In the ANA's 2023 survey of 162 members, owning, controlling and protecting first-party data was one of the stated reasons for moving work in-house. A small company can get the same protection without an in-house agency: open every account in its own name and grant access outward.

Regulation is moving the same way for the tools that hold the records. The EU Data Act's switching rules have applied since 12 September 2025 to cloud and SaaS providers serving EU customers. Contracts must allow a customer to start switching on no more than two months' notice, the switch must normally complete within 30 days, the data that can be exported must be specified, and from 12 January 2027 switching charges are prohibited. That helps with the CRM and the analytics stack. It does nothing for a spreadsheet in an ex-employee's personal drive, which is why the records row says shared, owned tools.

## If you bring in outside help

Write handover into the scope at the start, not the end. Accounts opened in your name. Reports in a format your team can produce without the agency. A final session that walks your team through every runbook. A good partner should be trying to make themselves unnecessary for the work they've finished.

| Clause | What it says | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Account ownership | All accounts opened in the company's name; agency granted access | Nobody can hold the company hostage with logins |
| Data and files | Raw data, creative source files and reports delivered and stored in company tools | The history stays when the agency goes |
| Reporting format | Reports the company's team can reproduce without the agency | Continuity after handover |
| Runbooks | Written procedures for each recurring task the agency performs | The work can continue or move |
| Handover session | A final walkthrough with the team that will take over | Tacit knowledge gets transferred |
| Decision record | The agency's reasons, including what it tried and dropped | The next team does not repeat failures |

The same discipline applies inside the company. Our piece on [the handover from sales to delivery](https://lowob.com/research/the-handover-from-sales-to-delivery/) shows where promises and reasons get lost between teams, and [what a system of record is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-of-record/) covers how to decide which tool is authoritative for each kind of data.

## The ten-question self-score

Score each question 0 to 5. Zero means "not at all"; five means "done, with evidence I could show an investor today."

| # | Question | Part |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Do fundraising, community and customer work run off one calendar with one owner? | 1 |
| 2 | Is there a one-sentence product truth, and a belief statement per audience? | 2 |
| 3 | Is there a dated evidence log with incentivised and organic activity separated? | 3 |
| 4 | Is the raise run from a researched list, tracked like a pipeline? | 4 |
| 5 | Does the community have a named job, measured by contribution? | 5 |
| 6 | Can you name the first hundred people who'd notice if you disappeared? | 6 |
| 7 | Do you have design partners with written success tests and agreed post-pilot prices? | 7 |
| 8 | Is every channel sorted open, restricted or closed, with partners ahead of paid media? | 8 |
| 9 | Do you report activation, retention, revenue, efficiency and source, instead of reach? | 9 |
| 10 | Would the system keep running if your most important person left tomorrow? | 10 |

**Reading your score (a rule of thumb, not a verdict):**

**40 to 50:** the system is in place. Spend on scale.

**30 to 39:** it works, with gaps. Fix the two lowest scores before the next big spend.

**Under 30:** you're likely spending on step eight with steps two and three unanswered. Go back to the lowest-numbered question you scored below 3 and start there.

**A zero on question 2, 3 or 7** is a stop sign regardless of total: no clear truth, no evidence or no real customer means the next dollar of fundraising or marketing is guesswork.

For teams launching a token, this sits alongside a stricter launch-readiness check covering legal, security, treasury and liquidity, which deserves its own piece.

## Closing the spine

The order matters more than any single tactic in these ten parts. Name the buyer. Write one truth. Collect evidence. Raise against it. Give your community a job. Make your first customers partners. Distribute through people who already have your buyer's trust. Measure what comes back. Then make sure you own all of it.

That's the whole system. Most teams have pieces of it. Very few have it in order.

## lowob takeaways

- **Own the accounts.** Every ad, social, email, analytics, domain and community admin account should be in the company's name.
- **Keep the reasons.** Three lines per major decision: what was chosen, what was rejected, what would change your mind.
- **Write handover in at the start.** Put it in an outside partner's scope on day one, not at the end.
- **Respect the stop signs.** A zero on product truth, evidence or real customers outranks the total score.

Gateway card

### The checklist

- Every account in the company's name, with an access list
- Evidence log, pipeline and monthly report in shared, owned tools
- Runbooks for the five most repeated GTM tasks
- A decision record for every major choice
- Handover written into every outside scope
- The ten-question self-score, done and dated
